explanations.answer: The Pharisees and all the Jews
explanations.explanation: That's what Mark says. In holding to the tradition of the elders, the Pharisees and all the Jews do not eat until they wash their hands ceremonially (Mark 7:3). The Pharisees are the strict religious leaders, and the writer says it's all the Jews, so this was a whole-community tradition. That's a lot of people washing before a meal.

explanations.answer: Only the priests at the temple
explanations.explanation: Good guess, but Mark casts a wider net. He says the Pharisees and all the Jews wash their hands ceremonially before they eat (Mark 7:3). The priests aren't mentioned at all in that verse. This habit reached way past the temple and into everybody's kitchen.

The scribes are standing right there in the scene, so I see why you picked them. But Mark says it's the Pharisees and all the Jews who wash their hands ceremonially before eating (Mark 7:3). That's a lot more people than a few visitors from Jerusalem. The whole community held to this tradition of the elders.

Close, but it's the opposite. Mark says that on returning from the market, they do not eat unless they wash (Mark 7:4). So the market trip adds a washing before the meal. Nobody walks in from the market and dives straight into dinner.

Right, it's false. Mark says that on returning from the market, they do not eat unless they wash (Mark 7:4). The market trip means a washing before the meal. I walk past a mixing bowl and just start stamping, so this level of routine impresses me.

explanations.answer: Why they skip the elders' tradition
explanations.explanation: Yes! They ask, "Why do Your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders?" (Mark 7:5). They add that the disciples eat with defiled hands. Some of them came all the way from Jerusalem (Mark 7:1) for THAT. Unwashed hands, baker. UNWASHED. HANDS. They hunted that like detectives who found one crumb and called it a crime scene.

explanations.answer: Why they work on the Sabbath
explanations.explanation: The Sabbath does come up in other places, like when Pharisees question Jesus about His disciples picking grain (Mark 2:23-24). But not here. In this scene they ask why the disciples do not walk according to the tradition of the elders, and they point to eating with defiled hands (Mark 7:5). This complaint is all about hands and tradition.

explanations.answer: Why they don't fast like others
explanations.explanation: Fasting is a real question people brought to Jesus in another place (Mark 2:18), but it's not on the table here. The Pharisees and scribes ask why His disciples do not walk according to the tradition of the elders, and they say the disciples eat with defiled hands (Mark 7:5). This complaint is about washing before a meal, not skipping one.

That's right. In the words Jesus quotes, "These people honor Me with their lips…" (Mark 7:6). It's the very next part that stings, because the quote goes on to say "…but their hearts are far from Me." (Mark 7:6). Honoring God with the lips while the heart is far from Him is exactly what Jesus is naming.

Careful, because this one is sneaky. The words Jesus quotes say, "These people honor Me with their lips…" (Mark 7:6). So the lips part is true. The sting comes right after, when the quote says their hearts are far from God.

Yes. The quote says, "They worship Me in vain; they teach as doctrine the precepts of men." (Mark 7:7). Precepts are rules, and these are rules that came from men. Jesus is pointing at the difference between what God said and what people added.

Not quite. The quote says they teach as doctrine "…the precepts of men." (Mark 7:7). That's the answer the verse gives, and the prophets' words aren't what it names. The trouble Jesus points to is rules that came from men.

I see the pull of that one, since Moses comes up later in this very scene. But the words Jesus quotes say they teach as doctrine "…the precepts of men." (Mark 7:7). Jesus will actually use Moses to show them where they've drifted (Mark 7:10). So the problem was rules made by men, not the law.

That's it. Jesus says, "You have disregarded the commandment of God to keep the tradition of men." (Mark 7:8). Two things are on the table, God's commandment and a tradition of men. Jesus says they dropped the first to hold the second.

The temple is a big part of life in this world, but Jesus doesn't mention it here. He says, "You have disregarded the commandment of God to keep the tradition of men." (Mark 7:8). The word that fits the blank is commandment. Their trouble was with what God commanded.

The Sabbath shows up in other Pharisee arguments, like in Mark 2:24, so it's a fair guess. But in this verse Jesus says, "You have disregarded the commandment of God to keep the tradition of men." (Mark 7:8). The Sabbath isn't in this verse at all. The word that fits is commandment.

That's what Jesus says. Once a man says it's Corban, he is no longer permitted to do anything for his father or mother (Mark 7:12). Not a little, not a bit. Nothing. That's how a tradition could undo "Honor your father and your mother…" (Mark 7:10).

That would be a gentler rule than the one Jesus describes. He says the man is no longer permitted to do anything for his father or mother (Mark 7:12). There's no leftovers clause in the text. The door is just closed.

A priest would make a tidy answer, but Jesus never brings one in. He says the man is no longer permitted to do anything for his father or mother (Mark 7:12). Nobody gets to approve a little exception. Under their tradition, the answer is nothing.

explanations.answer: Anything that enters him from outside
explanations.explanation: Yes. Jesus says, "Nothing that enters a man from the outside can defile him…" (Mark 7:15). That turns the whole handwashing argument on its head. The thing that counts isn't what goes in.

explanations.answer: Anything he says when he's angry
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, because Jesus does talk about what comes out of a man. He says the things that come out of a man are what defile him (Mark 7:15). But this question asks what can't defile, and Jesus says that's anything that enters a man from the outside. So this answer isn't the one Jesus names here.

Jesus never sorts things by secret or public here. He says, "Nothing that enters a man from the outside can defile him…" (Mark 7:15). That's the thing that can't defile. What comes out of a man is the other side of it.

That's right! Jesus says, "but the things that come out of a man, these are what defile him." (Mark 7:15). He says it to the crowd He called to Him. Everybody had been arguing about what goes IN, all that hands and washing talk. Then Jesus turns it around to what comes OUT, and I bet that crowd got quiet fast. It's like scrubbing the outside of a mixing bowl until it sparkles while nobody asks what's in the dough.

It's actually true. Jesus tells the crowd, "but the things that come out of a man, these are what defile him." (Mark 7:15). It's the flip side of the first half of His sentence, where nothing from the outside can defile. Same verse, two halves.

It's the other way around. Jesus says what enters a man from the outside "…does not enter his heart, but it goes into the stomach and then is eliminated." (Mark 7:19). So it never reaches the heart. The heart is where Jesus says the real trouble starts.

Right. Jesus says it "…does not enter his heart, but it goes into the stomach and then is eliminated." (Mark 7:19). The stomach gets it, and the heart doesn't. That's why the outside stuff can't defile a man the way what comes from within does.
Yes, clean. Mark adds, "(Thus all foods are clean.)" (Mark 7:19). It's the writer's own note after Jesus' words. Where I come from, that's good news for every cookie too.

Blessed sounds nice, but it's not the word Mark uses. The note says, "(Thus all foods are clean.)" (Mark 7:19). The word is clean, which fits the whole talk about what defiles. Jesus' point is that food doesn't make a man unclean.

That's the opposite of what Mark's note says. It reads, "(Thus all foods are clean.)" (Mark 7:19). Jesus has just said food goes to the stomach and not the heart. So nothing on that plate makes a man unclean.

explanations.answer: From within the hearts of men
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus says, "For from within the hearts of men come evil thoughts…" (Mark 7:21). The trouble comes from the heart, not from the plate. That's why scrubbing hands can't fix it.

It's a fair thought that other people would be the cause. But Jesus says, "For from within the hearts of men come evil thoughts…" (Mark 7:21). He points inward, not at the crowd. And He says it to the disciples in the house, away from the crowd (Mark 7:17).

Food is exactly what Jesus just ruled out. He says it goes into the stomach and is eliminated (Mark 7:19), and Mark adds, "(Thus all foods are clean.)" Then Jesus says, "For from within the hearts of men come evil thoughts…" (Mark 7:21). The source is the heart.
